entities.name: De Motu Cordis (On the Motion of the Heart and Blood)
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Published in 1628 by the English physician William Harvey (1578–1657), Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus (An Anatomical Exercise on the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals) is one of the most important works in the history of medicine. In a slim 72-page treatise, Harvey demolished the 1,400-year-old Galenic model (which held that blood was continuously produced in the liver and consumed by the body) by demonstrating through quantitative reasoning and systematic experiment that the heart is a pump that circulates blood in a closed loop through the body.

His key insight was mathematical: he calculated the volume of blood the heart pumps per hour (estimated at over 500 pounds) and showed it was impossibly large for continuous production — therefore, the same blood must circulate repeatedly. Harvey also correctly described the systemic and pulmonary circuits, though without a microscope he could not see the capillaries (discovered by Malpighi in 1661). De Motu Cordis is a landmark in the application of quantitative, experimental method to biology.
